  Terse gloss: "little ones, small children — collective noun for the young dependents of a household or community"
  Readable gloss: "Taf is a collective noun for small children, those who toddle and take quick, tripping steps — a vivid etymological image. It never appears in construct state or plural form, always designating children as a group. In the Pentateuch, taf regularly appears in lists of dependents alongside women and livestock when a community is on the move (Gen 46:5; Num 31:9). Deuteronomy uses it to mark those too young to have witnessed the exodus (Deut 1:39). The term can be gender-specific when modified: zakar battaf ('male among the little ones,' Num 31:17) and hattaf bannashim ('young girls,' Num 31:18). The translations consistently capture this: Spanish 'ninos,' French 'enfants,' German 'die Kleinen.'"

SENSES:
  Sense 1: "little ones, young children"
    Enriched: A collective term for young children and dependents, distinct from fighting or laboring adults. Appears in inventory-style enumerations — 'their little ones, their wives, and their livestock' (Gen 34:29; 46:5) — and in contexts specifying non-combatants (Num 31:9, 17-18). Never pluralized, never in construct. Judges 18:21 and 2 Samuel 15:22 confirm its use beyond the Pentateuch.
    Existing Spanish translations: Pero-vuestros-niños, Vuestros-niños, niños, niños-de-ellos, para-niños-vuestros, para-sus-niños, sus-niños, vuestros-niños, y-los-niños, y-niño, y-niños, y-vuestros-pequeños
